messages.author: e82d2514284339f5
messages.subject: Dynamically generating observers within observe()...?
parts:
Hi,

I am trying something that I'm not sure is really possible. See an executable example (with some things cut out) on gist:
https://gist.github.com/meowcat/5c4f80a9b173e56bcc22

The example is minimalized, of course. The gist of it is that with two sliders, input.x and input.y, I adjust the number of plots in a grid. In the actual application, I can then assign stuff to be plotted; I can then select a "compound" on the sidebar for which all that stuff would be plotted.

The plots are displayed with uiOutput, which is a dynamically generated output with named plots. This was adapted from something I found here: https://gist.github.com/wch/5436415

By and large this works great, but what I have trouble with is that I want to catch clicks on the plots.

The output element with the plots is built as follows:
  # Insert the right number of plot output objects into the web page
  output$plots <- renderUI({
    r.y <- lapply(1:input$panel.y, function(panels.y)
    {
      r.x <- lapply(1:input$panel.x, function(panels.x)
        {
        plotname <- paste("plot",panels.x,panels.y, sep="-")
        clickname <- paste(plotname, "click", sep="-")
        column(width= 12/input$panel.x, plotOutput(plotname, clickId=clickname))
      })
      do.call(fixedRow, r.x)
    })
    #do.call(tagList, r.x)
  })
 
The plot itself is plotted as follows:
  # The actual plotting function

  observe({

    # replot on change of panel settings

    input$panel.x

    input$panel.y

    

    # replot on selecting a new compound

    input$cpd

    row <- as.integer(input$cpd)

    # note: in reality, I also replot in other cases. 


    for(panels.y in 1:input$panel.y) {

      for(panels.x in 1:input$panel.x) {

        

        local({

          

          inputname <- paste("file",panels.x,panels.y, sep="-")

          plotname <- paste("plot",panels.x,panels.y, sep="-")

 

          output[[plotname]] <- renderPlot({

            plot.new()

            title(main=paste(inputname, row)) 


          })

        

        }) #local

      } # for panels.x

    } # for panels.y

 

  }) # observe

This works great, but the "clickname" part is new. What I have to do now, is to dynamically build observers for every clickId when the panel.x or panel.y are changed. An observe() within an observe() doesn't really work and I am basically just trying random combinations of observe() isolate() reactive() and such, since I have not a deep enough understanding of the interdependencies that I would be able to approach this with an actual concept :). The one in the code right now is of course not working. Does anyone of you have experience with something like this?

What I believe would work, is to pre-generate observers for the maximum number of plots possible, which will just not be triggered as long as there are no plots there. (Hm, can you actually generate a dependency on an input which doesn't exist yet?) However this would be boring and not elegant, I'm really looking for the clean way to dynamically generate the observer when it is needed... Or some other "nice" solution...

Thanks for any help!

messages.author: ca443e6eaa0e78ed
messages.subject: Re: Dynamically generating observers within observe()...?
parts:
You CAN nest observers, in fact. Just be aware that each time the outer observer runs, it's creating a new set of observers (while the previously created observers continue to exist and run). So I'd keep track of the sets of observers you've already created, and when input$panel.y/input$panel.x change, just create the ones that don't yet exist.

Also just because you asked, yes, you can generate a dependency on an input which doesn't exist yet. If you call input$foo it'll just be NULL, and when it later gets set you'll be notified.

And finally just because I have a feeling this might be relevant to you in the future, when you call observe() you actually get an object back that can be used to suspend, resume, or destroy the observer. See ?observe for details.
